title: Three Maps
subtitle: Orient yourself, understand the terrain, choose a destination
summary: Pip finds three maps. The locator shows where the work fits; the topographic map reveals organizational terrain and decision paths; the treasure map connects today’s position to a shared destination. Comparing them keeps the workshop’s nearest problem from becoming its only priority.

concepts.title: Locator map
concepts.body: The payment team waves Pip over: their problem feels like the whole workshop. Pip opens the locator map and zooms out. Which company goal does this project serve? How large is it in the wider landscape, and whose perspective is missing? Locating ownership helps, but orientation also means judging relative importance. The nearest problem is not automatically the organization’s most important one.

steps.text: Pip steps back from the loudest nearby request.
Locate the project and its ownership.
Compare its importance with other needs and perspectives.

concepts.title: Topographic map
concepts.body: The org chart gives Pip a route that never reaches approval. A colleague sketches another: informal influence, the actual decision forum, and a security expert absent from the chart. This is the topographic map. Past experiences and cultural hazards help explain resistance. Pip compares maps with others, learning who holds knowledge and where decisions happen rather than mistaking reporting lines for the whole terrain.

steps.text: Pip checks where decisions actually happen.
Formal reporting lines provide only part of the map.
The actual approval path explains the bottleneck.

concepts.title: Treasure map
concepts.body: Pip draws a flag over “safe independent releases.” The treasure map needs more than a destination: where is the workshop now, and what is the next part of the route? Colleagues mark obstacles and discuss a detour. The map makes direction and progress discussable. It is not a promise that every hazard is known or that reaching the flag will follow the first line drawn.

concepts.title: Local maximum
concepts.body: A local cache makes one team faster but blocks the shared reliability plan. Pip steps back from the glowing team metric. A local maximum improves the nearby situation while making the wider destination harder to reach; downstream colleagues may carry the extra work. The answer may be coordination or a different objective, not harder optimization. Pip asks what improves the workshop’s outcome, not just this corner.

steps.text: Pip checks who pays for a local improvement.
A cache improves one team’s metric.
Judge the change against the shared destination.

misconceptions.claim: a staff-plus role is mainly about applying a universal formula.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter treats judgment as contextual: identify forces, listen to evidence, and adapt the response to the actual system and people.

misconceptions.claim: A visible activity or artifact proves the work is complete.
misconceptions.correction: Completion requires a useful outcome, shared understanding, and a way to notice whether the decision worked over time.

scenario.title: Reconcile the maps
scenario.context: Pip’s locator map prioritizes payments. An identity dependency looks fragile; the topographic map reveals security approval as the bottleneck. The owners see different routes.

options.label: Reconcile maps
options.benefit: Owners can address the dependency and approval path together.
options.cost: The visible payment fix waits while the owners compare constraints.
options.consequence: Pip brings the owners together; their combined maps reveal a route through identity and security approval.

options.label: Follow the loudest map
options.benefit: The loudest team sees a quick local fix.
options.cost: The underlying identity and approval constraints remain.
options.consequence: Payments changes, but the next project meets the same bottleneck. Pip’s busy quarter has not changed the terrain.

scenario.debrief: The maps answer different questions. Pip needs their combined perspective to avoid a local fix that leaves the shared destination out of reach.

quiz.question: Which map reveals informal decision paths and cultural terrain?
quiz.explanation: The terrain includes how influence and decisions actually travel.

quiz.question: What does the treasure map contribute?
options: A destination and a route from the current position
A list of every production metric
quiz.explanation: It connects where the organization is with where it wants to go.

quiz.question: A team improves its own throughput but delays every dependent team. What is missing?
options: A view of the wider organizational outcome
quiz.explanation: The locator map helps challenge local optimization that harms the broader goal.

exercise.title: Make the next move legible
exercise.prompt: Describe a staff-level decision, the people and terrain involved, and the route by which you will learn whether it worked.

fields.label: What does each map reveal?
fields.placeholder: Write the concrete facts, people, and constraint.

fields.label: Where do the maps disagree?
fields.placeholder: State the choice and its trade-off.

fields.label: Who can validate the terrain?
fields.placeholder: Name the evidence or conversation that will revisit it.
